paras: The scene that made the book famous takes four pages and, by the author's own account, never happened. He had been working on the memoir for six years when a cousin wrote to him with a photograph. In the scene as published he is nine years old, standing in a kitchen doorway on a winter afternoon in 1974 while his father packs a suitcase; the light, the smell of the coat and the sound of the latch are all there, and readers who remember nothing else about the book remember that kitchen. The photograph showed the same kitchen in the same year. His father had left in April, and the family had moved out of the house eighteen months before the winter he describes. The memory was vivid, complete and, in every checkable respect, false.

What is unusual here is not the error but the paper trail. Psychologists had been demonstrating for decades that memory is not storage but reconstruction -- that we rebuild a scene every time we look back on it, borrowing detail from photographs, from other people's accounts, and from whatever the story has needed to mean. Very few of us ever find the receipt. Anybody who takes witness statements knows the same pattern from the other side: a person who is trying hard to be honest, who was standing in the right place, and whose backstory has been quietly reorganised by everything that happened afterwards. The aftermath rewrites the event. By the time the statement is taken three years have often passed, and the witness has told the story forty times, each telling smoothing it a little further.

The interesting question is what to do with an account once you know how it is made, and the answer is not to throw it away. The author kept the chapter and added four pages explaining what the photograph showed. The book is better for it: what had been a moving scene became a moving scene plus an argument about memory, and the twist is that the second version is the more truthful book. In a courtroom as much as on a page, a statement that says where the certainty ends is worth more than one that glosses over the gaps. What cannot survive is the version that presents a reconstruction as a recording. Everything unravels from there -- not because the person lied, but because nobody, the person included, can now tell which parts were remembered and which were built.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: The author invented the scene deliberately, and memoirs should not be trusted.
An account is not worthless once you know memory is reconstructive -- what fails is presenting a reconstruction as a recording, and the honest version says where the certainty ends.
Witness statements are more reliable than memoirs, because they are taken under oath.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: By the time I reached chapter nine, the narrator had already lied to me twice.
I was reading the memoir on a plane when I realized I had met one of the people in it.
She had been writing the book for eleven years before anybody saw a page of it.
In hindsight, the twist had been in front of me since the first chapter.
He glosses over the year that mattered most, and the aftermath takes up half the book.
Looking back on it now, what I remember is not what happened but how it was told.

listenings.text: I have never once told a story in the order it happened, and I have stopped apologising for it. The reason is not literary, it is practical. If I begin at the beginning, the reader has to carry forty pages of backstory before anything is at stake, and nobody carries it. They put the book down at page nine and they are very polite about it later. So I start in the middle of a bad afternoon, and then, once the reader already wants to know why this woman is sitting in a car outside her own house, I go back. That is the moment the past perfect earns its keep. She had left that morning. She had been planning it for a year. And the year arrives as an explanation rather than as homework. My editor tells me I overuse the device, and she is right, and I am going to keep doing it, because the alternative is a book that nobody finishes.

When I take a statement about something that happened three years ago, I do not start with the event. I start with the day around it. What you were doing that morning, what the weather was like, who else was in the building, whether you had eaten. It sounds like small talk and it is not. Two things happen. The first is that the ordinary detail brings the rest back, because memory is stored next to the boring parts, not next to the dramatic ones. The second is that it shows me quite quickly which sections are remembered and which are reconstructed, and that distinction is worth more to me than confidence is. A witness who says he cannot remember whether the door was open is a better witness than one who is certain about everything, and any judge who has been doing the job for a while knows it too.
